description: Sentiment track, SG04: minimal pairs as SG03 (pairs_targeted_v1), but the types come from the SR02 errors on the official TEST set (D-023, test-contaminated; Ammar 2026-11-02). Types agreed with Ammar on 2026-11-02 after his review of the candidates (data/inspect/hard_cases/sg04_type_candidates.md, sg04_review_ammar.csv): sarcastic praise, public jab, personal remark, prayer, emoji in context; spam hashtags dropped. Labels follow Ammar's reading, not the test gold where they differ: sincere praise or encouragement is POS; disapproval or reproach without negative words is NEG. Few-shot pairs: one side (or both) is a real S1-train tweet (ids in `source_ids`; never a test tweet), the other side was written by Claude and is NOT yet checked by Ammar. Placeholders as v1: {task} {examples} {variety_name} {variety_instruction} {hint}.
system: You are an Arabic-speaking social media user who writes posts on Twitter.

msa.name: Modern Standard Arabic
msa.instruction: Use Modern Standard Arabic (Fusha), not a dialect.

egypt.name: Egyptian Arabic
egypt.instruction: Use the Egyptian dialect, not Modern Standard Arabic.

gulf.name: Gulf Arabic
gulf.instruction: Use the Gulf dialect (as spoken in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain or Oman), not Modern Standard Arabic.

levant.name: Levantine Arabic
levant.instruction: Use the Levantine dialect (as spoken in Syria, Lebanon, Jordan or Palestine), not Modern Standard Arabic.

sarcastic_praise.task:
Write a pair of tweets about the same subject that both use words of praise or congratulation.
Tweet A means the praise sincerely: the writer is really pleased, proud or thankful, so its sentiment is positive.
Tweet B keeps the same words of praise but uses them sarcastically: the writer is mocking or criticising the subject, and the praise means the opposite, so its sentiment is negative.

public_jab.task:
Write a pair of tweets about the same public matter: politics, sports, news or public services.
Tweet A only states the matter or asks about it, in a plain tone, with no opinion and no feeling, so its sentiment is neutral.
Tweet B is about the same matter but adds a dig at the people responsible: a sarcastic joke, an ironic question or a mocking comparison. It may contain no negative words at all; the dig itself makes its sentiment negative.

personal_remark.task:
Write a pair of short, informal tweets in dialect about the same everyday moment in the writer's own life: their day, their family, friends, work or study. Each under 20 words.
Tweet A only tells what happened or what the writer wants, or makes a light joke about it, with no blame and no complaint, so its sentiment is neutral.
Tweet B is about the same moment, but the writer shows real annoyance, blame or disapproval of someone, even without strong negative words (a reproach or a pointed question is enough), so its sentiment is negative.

prayer.task:
Write a pair of tweets built around the same prayer, supplication or Quran verse.
Tweet A only quotes or says the prayer, with nothing about the writer's own feelings, so its sentiment is neutral.
Tweet B has the same prayer, but the writer adds their own joy, gratitude or happiness about something in their life, so its sentiment is positive.

emoji_context.task:
Write a pair of short tweets that both use the same emoji, such as 😭 or 😂💔, about the same subject.
In tweet A the emoji shows excitement, love or laughter: the writer is thrilled or delighted, so its sentiment is positive.
In tweet B the same emoji shows real sadness or disappointment: something went wrong for the writer, so its sentiment is negative. Only the context decides the sentiment, not the emoji.
